peak_estimate.note: The current level is already above every analogue on these same days, so both adding and multiplying their gain lead beyond anything measured (record of the series +3.02 °C). The real question is not how much higher but when the growth stops: for the analogues that happened in November or December.

roni.note: RONI is the Niño 3.4 anomaly minus the mean anomaly of the whole tropics (20°S–20°N). NOAA switched its classification to it in February 2026 because a warm tropical ocean makes the plain ONI overstate how strongly the atmosphere is being pushed. The gap between the two is the warm background this event runs on.

breakdown.note: per issue: models whose nearest verifiable forecast came in below the ONI that season actually had

todate.note: the models forecast a three-month mean; this compares them with the part of that season already measured, so a model below this number would need the rest of the season to be colder than the part already lived

live.note: Root-mean-square over the models that kept up with reality (the mean is kept alongside for reference): squaring gives the strong forecasts the weight they deserve, because a single model calling a much larger peak is news, not noise. Weighted mean over the models that kept up with reality: broken ones are out entirely, chronic laggards enter with a small weight, unverified ones with half. The published plume average counts all of them equally.

iri.position_note: Where we stand is read off the seasons we have actually lived, not off the first season the models publish: the plume starts at ASO, but by then only 1 of its 3 months are measured. For seasons the models do not publish (JJA, JAS) the spread of the unmeasured months is BORROWED from the nearest forecast season — an assumption, not a measurement.

risks.title: A very strong El Niño is under way
risks.evidence: Niño 3.4 by the NOAA weekly index +2.6 °C on 2026-08-26; daily OISST +2.65. Among all years since 1982 for the same 30 days: rank 1.
risks.plain: Water in the key patch of the Pacific is 2.6 degrees warmer than normal. The threshold for a “very strong” event is two degrees. This is not a forecast, it is already measured, and it has never happened this early in the year.
risks.watch: the NOAA weekly index; the official ONI is now +1.80 (JJA), the “very strong” category starts at +2.0 on the three-month average

risks.title: The fuel is at its record and has not started to burn
risks.evidence: Warm water volume 3.24·10¹⁴ m³, 100 % of the highest value of the series since 1980; the peak was this month. On our own data this gauge leads the surface index by 6 months.
risks.plain: The heat that will surface later is already piled up under the equator, and it is at a record for the whole series. This is measured, not forecast: the surface has not yet shown what is already stored below. While the gauge is not falling, the event has something to grow on.
risks.watch: the monthly PMEL update: the first clear fall of the volume is the earliest honest sign that the peak is near

risks.title: Water +11.3 °C above normal is sitting at 100 m under 125°W
risks.evidence: TAO mooring 125°W, five-day mean to 2026-09-01, against the mooring's own 1991–2020 record. The 20 °C isotherm is at 166.7 m in the west and 130.2 m in the east.
risks.plain: This is the heat that has not surfaced yet. It is measured directly, every day, and it is what makes 'the event has room to grow' a statement about the present rather than about the past events.
risks.watch: the warm anomaly moving east along the moorings and rising toward the surface; the east D20 shallowing again would mean the wave has passed

risks.title: The event has room to grow: the fuel is charged and the analogues peaked in winter
risks.evidence: Past analogues peaked in November to January. Adding their gain from the same date gives +3.2 … +4.5 °C, above the record of the series +3.02.
risks.plain: Every past event of this strength peaked in winter, November to January. It is the end of summer now, so two or three more months of growth are likely. How much higher cannot be said: we are already above anything the ocean has shown at this time of year, and past events are no guide here. The real question is when the growth stops.
risks.watch: if the weekly Niño 3.4 stops rising before November, the event has reached its plateau earlier than the analogues

risks.title: The eastern Pacific is heating, off the coast of South America
risks.evidence: Niño 1+2 +4.2, Niño 4 +1.0: difference +3.2 °C.
risks.plain: There are two kinds of El Niño: one heats the middle of the ocean, the other the east, off Peru and Ecuador. This is the second kind, the harshest in its consequences: 1982 and 1997 were like this. Such events brought downpours and floods to the coast of South America and droughts to Indonesia and Australia.
risks.watch: the difference staying above 1 °C through September and October

risks.title: The world ocean is warmer every day than it has ever been on that day
risks.evidence: 30 record days out of the last 30, a run of 30 days in a row; 108 of 247 days this year.
risks.plain: On each of the last 30 days the ocean, averaged over the planet, was warmer than on the same day of any year since 1982. Not one hot day, but an unbroken stretch.
risks.watch: the first day below the record without a change of season is the first sign of a turn

risks.title: Niño 3.4: not a spike but a new level
risks.evidence: accumulated shift +147 against a threshold of 5; first over the threshold 94 days ago
risks.plain: The series did not jump and come back; it rose and stayed. The gauge that accumulates the excess over the spring level crossed its threshold 94 days ago and has only grown since.
risks.watch: if the accumulated gauge starts to fall, the regime is letting go

risks.title: The year after the peak: 2027 is likely to be warmer than 2026
risks.evidence: In 1982→1983 +0.19 °C, 1997→1998 +0.19 °C, 2015→2016 +0.18 °C, 2023→2024 +0.12 °C (annual land+ocean mean, ERA5); warmer in 4 of 4 analogues, median +0.19.
risks.plain: El Niño releases the ocean's heat into the air with a lag of a few months, so the calendar year that follows the peak is usually the warmer one. That is why 1998, 2016 and 2024 each became the warmest year measured up to that point. On the same arithmetic, next year is the one to plan for, not this one.
risks.watch: annual land+ocean mean once the peak passes; the first months of next year already carry the signal

risks.title: The air is answering the ocean, so the event can travel
risks.evidence: Southern Oscillation Index -1.1, convection at the date line -1.0 standard deviations, trade wind in the west -2.0. 3 of 3 atmospheric signs are in place.
risks.plain: El Niño is not a warm patch of water, it is a coupling: the water heats, the trade winds give way, the cloud tower moves east, and only then does the event reach harvests on the other side of the planet. All three are in place now, which is why the regional impacts on this page are worth taking seriously.
risks.watch: the same three: if the winds return and the convection moves back west, the event stays in the ocean and the teleconnections fade

risks.title: The upper 300 m of the central and eastern Pacific hold +2.51 °C of extra heat
risks.evidence: GODAS reanalysis, 2026-07: mean temperature anomaly of 0–300 m across 180–100°W, our climatology; the reanalysis' warmest point is 9.19 °C at 75.0 m, 104.5°W.
risks.plain: The CPC calls this the upper-ocean heat content index and watches it as the leading sign of where the surface goes next. A whole degree across that band is a large charge.
risks.watch: the index in the next monthly GODAS; the moorings above show it a month earlier

risks.title: world ocean: not a spike but a new level
risks.evidence: accumulated shift +55 against a threshold of 5; first over the threshold 60 days ago
risks.plain: The series did not jump and come back; it rose and stayed. The gauge that accumulates the excess over the spring level crossed its threshold 60 days ago and has only grown since.
risks.watch: if the accumulated gauge starts to fall, the regime is letting go

risks.title: land+ocean: not a spike but a new level
risks.evidence: accumulated shift +30 against a threshold of 5; first over the threshold 33 days ago
risks.plain: The series did not jump and come back; it rose and stayed. The gauge that accumulates the excess over the spring level crossed its threshold 33 days ago and has only grown since.
risks.watch: if the accumulated gauge starts to fall, the regime is letting go

risks.title: world ocean: the last 30 days are the warmest in the whole record
risks.evidence: anomaly +0.74 °C, rank 1 of 45; above trend +0.33 (z = 3.32)
risks.plain: For these same dates none of the 45 years was warmer. Even after subtracting the general warming, +0.33 degrees remain above it: that is what the event itself adds.
risks.watch: whether the lead holds after the change of season

risks.title: land+ocean: the last 30 days are the warmest in the whole record
risks.evidence: anomaly +0.83 °C, rank 1 of 87; above trend +0.53 (z = 2.83)
risks.plain: For these same dates none of the 87 years was warmer. Even after subtracting the general warming, +0.53 degrees remain above it: that is what the event itself adds.
risks.watch: whether the lead holds after the change of season

risks.title: Some forecast models are already below reality
risks.evidence: 10 of 26 models gave less for ASO than the already reached +2.6 °C: CPC MRKOV, CS-IRI-MM, CSU CLIPR, IAP-NN, IOCAS ICM, JAMSTEC CNN…. Model mean +2.77, spread +1.60…+3.75.
risks.plain: Of 26 models, 10 have already fallen behind what the ocean showed this week. They are not “wrong about the future”; they are not keeping up with the present. Their winter forecasts are most likely too low.
risks.watch: the next IRI issue: how many models catch up

metric.name: Combined forecast peak by IRI issue

risks.title: The models are revising the forecast upward for the second month running
risks.evidence: Since the Jul 2026 issue 25 of 25 models raised their peak, 0 lowered it; combined peak +2.95 → +3.25 °C.
risks.plain: When almost all models move their forecast in the same direction, the event is outrunning them. The shift itself is a signal: the next issue will probably be higher again.
risks.watch: the IRI issue around the 19th

metric.name: Combined forecast peak by IRI issue

risks.title: A La Niña usually follows within a year or two
risks.evidence: After the analogues the ONI fell to 1982: -1.06, 1997: -1.53, 2015: -0.76, 2023: -0.61; it crossed the La Niña threshold of −0.5 in 4 of 4 cases.
risks.plain: The ocean does not simply return to normal: after a strong El Niño it usually swings the other way. A La Niña flips the map of impacts, so the regions that are dry now tend to be wet then, and the grain exporters that had a good year tend to have a bad one. Planning that only covers this winter misses the swing.
risks.watch: the ONI trend after the peak; a fall of 0.3 or more per month is the usual signature of the swing

risks.title: Global temperature in 2027 is likely to run above 2026; regional impacts follow their own lags
risks.evidence: Land+ocean is +0.53 °C above trend now, while the ocean heat that drives it is still rising; in the analogues the air-temperature records, the harvest failures and the price effects all came in the year after the onset.
risks.plain: The dashboard measures the ocean today, but people meet an El Niño through harvests, water and prices, and those arrive with a delay of six to eighteen months. The plans that matter are for next year: import contracts, reserves, water rationing, insurance.
risks.watch: the first harvests after the peak season and the food price index six to twelve months from the onset

risks.title: The atmosphere is still catching up, by three floors
risks.evidence: Satellite lower troposphere in the tropics +0.90 °C; on our own data this layer follows Niño 3.4 with a delay of 3 months (correlation 0.69).
risks.plain: The ocean heats the air, not the other way round, and the air takes months to answer. That is why the warmest months of the whole record usually arrive AFTER the peak of an El Niño, not during it — and why the year that follows this one is the one to watch.
risks.watch: the monthly satellite layers: the tropics react first, the global mean follows

risks.title: 2 westerly wind bursts in the last 120 days, the latest 13 days ago
risks.evidence: 2026-06-30 to 2026-07-06 (7 d, peak 6.75 m/s); 2026-08-14 to 2026-08-21 (8 d, peak 5.2 m/s). Threshold 4.11 m/s = two sigma of the daily anomaly. Last week: 3.4 m/s.
risks.plain: Bursts are how an El Niño is fed: the warm water each one sends east surfaces off South America two to three months later. The bursts of the last four months are the ones arriving now and through the autumn.
risks.watch: a new run of five days above the threshold; the MJO entering phases 6–8 makes one more likely

risks.title: The ocean holds more heat than ever measured (0–2000 m)
risks.evidence: 33.97 × 10²² J in 2026 Q1, a record of the series since 1955; up 11.2 in ten years.
risks.plain: This is the reservoir the event draws on and returns to. A record reservoir means the statistical forecasts, trained on a cooler ocean, are reading a different system than the one they learned.
risks.watch: the next quarterly NCEI update; whether the 0–2000 m series keeps rising through the event

food.note: FAO Food Price Index, 2014–16 = 100; published the first Friday of the month for the previous month.

season_notes.SON: September-October-November. The season when El Niño is building towards its peak: the teleconnections are already switched on, and in the southern hemisphere it is the planting season.
season_notes.DJF: December-January-February. The peak season of almost every El Niño and the strongest teleconnections: the southern African and Australian summer, the northern winter.
season_notes.MAM: March-April-May. The decaying phase: the ocean is still warm, and the food consequences of the peak season arrive as harvests and prices.

base.what: the event peaks near the middle of the plume, counting only the models that kept up

strong.what: the event peaks at the top of the spread of the models that kept up

record.what: the peak goes above the record of the weekly NOAA series

scenario_support._note: Share of the 14 IRI models whose peak reaches the threshold — counting only the models that kept up with reality; the ones that broke are left out, because a forecast already below the lived part of the season cannot set the scale for the ones ahead. Not a probability: these are 14 different models, not draws from one. Reality is already above 0 of them, so every share here is a lower bound.

items.name: Gulf and Arabian Peninsula
items.countries: UAE, Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, Qatar, Oman, Bahrain, Yemen

SON.note: The winter rain season has not started; no consistent signal.

DJF.note: El Niño strengthens the subtropical jet over Arabia, and winter rainfall runs above normal: the documented pathway behind heavy-rain and flash-flood episodes on the peninsula, including the April 2024 Gulf floods.

MAM.note: The wet tendency fades through spring; heat arrives early.

vulnerability.note: The Gulf states import 80–90 % of their food and grow almost no cereals: the exposure is entirely to world prices, shipping and the harvests of exporters. Yemen combines that dependence with an ongoing food emergency.

actions: Flood preparedness: drainage, protect stored grain, health measures for water-borne disease, early warning for river basins.
Forward-contract cereal imports, build strategic reserves, budget for price rises, target social safety nets.

items.name: East Africa
items.countries: Kenya, Somalia, southern Ethiopia, Tanzania, Uganda

SON.note: Short rains (Oct–Dec) usually well above normal; flooding and landslides, and conditions that favour desert locust breeding.

DJF.note: The wet tail of the short rains runs into January; standing water and disease follow.

MAM.note: The long rains show no consistent El Niño signal.

vulnerability.note: Large food-insecure population; cereal imports are 20–40 % of consumption in Kenya and Somalia; floods hit pastoral and lowland cropping areas hardest.

actions: Flood preparedness: drainage, protect stored grain, health measures for water-borne disease, early warning for river basins.
Forward-contract cereal imports, build strategic reserves, budget for price rises, target social safety nets.

items.name: Southern Africa
items.countries: Zimbabwe, Zambia, Malawi, Mozambique, South Africa, Botswana, Namibia

SON.note: A late and weak start of the rainy season delays planting.

DJF.note: The main maize season runs drier and hotter than normal: 1982-83, 1991-92, 2015-16 and 2023-24 all brought regional maize failures.

MAM.note: Rains end early and the harvest is cut short.

vulnerability.note: Maize-dependent diets and thin reserves; Zimbabwe, Malawi and Zambia declared drought emergencies in 2024.

actions: Pre-position drought-tolerant seed and fodder, plan water rationing, protect livestock, contract grain imports early.
Forward-contract cereal imports, build strategic reserves, budget for price rises, target social safety nets.

items.name: Pacific Islands
items.countries: Fiji, Papua New Guinea highlands, Vanuatu, Kiribati, Tuvalu, Micronesia

SON.note: The western Pacific (PNG, Fiji, Vanuatu) runs dry while the central Pacific (Kiribati, Tuvalu) is much wetter; sea level drops in the west and exposes reefs.

DJF.note: Drought in the west persists, and tropical cyclone activity shifts east towards French Polynesia and the Cooks.

vulnerability.note: Small islands import most staples and depend on shipping; the 1997-98 event brought famine conditions to the PNG highlands.

actions: Pre-position drought-tolerant seed and fodder, plan water rationing, protect livestock, contract grain imports early.

SON.note: The dry corridor (Guatemala, Honduras, El Salvador, Nicaragua) runs dry and the second bean and maize crop is at risk.

DJF.note: The Caribbean is drier than normal.

MAM.note: A late start of the first rainy season.

vulnerability.note: Haiti and the dry-corridor countries combine high import dependence with chronic food insecurity and out-migration.

items.name: Southeast Asia and Indonesia
items.countries: Indonesia, Philippines, Malaysia, Thailand, Vietnam, Papua New Guinea

SON.note: A delayed monsoon onset, drought and peat fires in Indonesia and Malaysia; the Philippines run dry.

DJF.note: Reduced rainfall persists; rice and palm-oil yields fall and Philippine drought deepens.

MAM.note: A dry tail: reservoirs low, hydropower reduced.

vulnerability.note: Rice self-sufficiency is thin in Indonesia and the Philippines, and both import in El Niño years; Thailand and Vietnam are exporters whose smaller crops raise world prices.

actions: Pre-position drought-tolerant seed and fodder, plan water rationing, protect livestock, contract grain imports early.

items.name: Peru, Ecuador and the Andes

SON.note: Coastal Ecuador and northern Peru begin to see heavy rain; the coastal El Niño effect is strongest in eastern-type events.

DJF.note: Torrential rain and floods on the Peruvian and Ecuadorian coast, as in 1982-83, 1997-98 and 2017; the anchoveta fishery collapses while the Bolivian altiplano and the southern Peruvian Andes run dry.

MAM.note: Coastal floods persist through the southern autumn, with landslides and disease outbreaks.

vulnerability.note: Peru imports wheat and maize; fishmeal exports and coastal agriculture (rice, mango, asparagus) are hit directly, and Colombia and Bolivia rely on imported wheat.

actions: Flood preparedness: drainage, protect stored grain, health measures for water-borne disease, early warning for river basins.
Prepare for a collapse of coastal upwelling fisheries: fishing bans, income support, alternative supply of fish protein.

items.name: South Asia
items.countries: India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka, Nepal

SON.note: The monsoon withdraws earlier; the north-east monsoon is mixed, and southern India and Sri Lanka are often wetter.

DJF.note: A warmer and drier winter in northern India and Pakistan; the rabi wheat crop is exposed to March heat.

MAM.note: Pre-monsoon heat waves become more likely.

vulnerability.note: Largely self-sufficient in cereals but with a huge population close to the margin; India restricts exports in bad years, and that alone moves world rice prices.

items.name: East Asia

SON.note: Southern China is somewhat wetter in autumn.

DJF.note: A wetter winter in southern China and a milder winter in Japan and Korea.

MAM.note: A wetter spring in south China; the following summer often brings Yangtze flooding, as in 1998 and 2016.

vulnerability.note: China holds large reserves but is the largest soybean and a major maize importer; Japan and Korea import most of their cereals but are wealthy enough to secure them.

actions: Flood preparedness: drainage, protect stored grain, health measures for water-borne disease, early warning for river basins.

items.name: Southern Cone
items.countries: southern Brazil, Uruguay, Paraguay, northern Argentina; north-east Brazil

SON.note: Southern Brazil, Uruguay and north-east Argentina run wetter, with floods in the Paraná basin, while north-east Brazil runs dry.

DJF.note: A wet summer favourable for Argentine soybean and maize once the floods drain; north-east Brazil stays in drought.

MAM.note: A wet autumn delays the harvest.

vulnerability.note: Net exporters of soybean, maize and wheat: the world-price effect is usually favourable because the crops are bigger, and the local risk is floods and the north-eastern drought.

actions: Flood preparedness: drainage, protect stored grain, health measures for water-borne disease, early warning for river basins.

items.name: Australia and New Zealand
items.countries: eastern and northern Australia, New Zealand

SON.note: Spring is drier and hotter in the east and north; the winter crop finishes badly and the bushfire season starts early.

DJF.note: A hot, dry summer in the east, bushfires, and a delayed northern wet season.

vulnerability.note: A major wheat exporter: a poor Australian crop tightens the world wheat balance and raises prices for importers elsewhere.

actions: Pre-position drought-tolerant seed and fodder, plan water rationing, protect livestock, contract grain imports early.
sources: NOAA CPC, El Niño and La Niña: typical global impacts (warm-episode maps, DJF and JJA), cpc.ncep.noaa.gov/products/analysis_monitoring/impacts
IRI, ENSO impacts by region and season, iri.columbia.edu/our-expertise/climate/enso

items.name: North America

SON.note: Weak autumn signals; the Atlantic hurricane season is usually suppressed.

DJF.note: The southern tier from California to Florida runs wetter, the northern US and Canada warmer and drier; the Pacific North-west and the Ohio valley run dry.

MAM.note: A wet spring in the southern Plains and the Gulf, which is good for winter wheat.

vulnerability.note: The largest maize and soybean exporter; El Niño winters are usually favourable for US crops, which eases world supply.

actions: Flood preparedness: drainage, protect stored grain, health measures for water-borne disease, early warning for river basins.
sources: NOAA CPC, El Niño and La Niña: typical global impacts (warm-episode maps, DJF and JJA), cpc.ncep.noaa.gov/products/analysis_monitoring/impacts
IRI, ENSO impacts by region and season, iri.columbia.edu/our-expertise/climate/enso

items.name: West Africa (Gulf of Guinea)

SON.note: No consistent signal for the second rainy season.

MAM.note: A weak and mixed signal at the start of the first rainy season.

vulnerability.note: Rice and wheat imports matter (Nigeria, Ghana); the exposure runs through world prices rather than local weather.

actions: No strong signal: watch the neighbours' harvests and world prices rather than local weather.
sources: NOAA CPC, El Niño and La Niña: typical global impacts (warm-episode maps, DJF and JJA), cpc.ncep.noaa.gov/products/analysis_monitoring/impacts
IRI, ENSO impacts by region and season, iri.columbia.edu/our-expertise/climate/enso
FAO / WTO list of Net Food-Importing Developing Countries; FAO cereal import dependency ratios (FAOSTAT food balances)

items.name: Europe

SON.note: Autumn shows no reliable El Niño signal over Europe.

DJF.note: Early winter is dominated by the North Atlantic, not the Pacific: the El Niño signal is weak and inconsistent between events.

MAM.note: Late winter and early spring carry the clearest, still weak, signal: a stratospheric pathway that tends towards a negative North Atlantic Oscillation, which usually means colder and drier northern Europe and wetter southern Europe and the Mediterranean.

vulnerability.note: A net exporter of cereals overall and wealthy enough to outbid others on the world market; the risk here is price, not availability. A poor southern-European harvest raises world prices for the importers elsewhere.

actions: Flood preparedness: drainage, protect stored grain, health measures for water-borne disease, early warning for river basins.
sources: Brönnimann 2007, Impact of El Niño–Southern Oscillation on European climate, Reviews of Geophysics 45; Ineson & Scaife 2009, the stratospheric pathway to late-winter Europe, Nature Geoscience 2
NOAA CPC, El Niño and La Niña: typical global impacts (warm-episode maps, DJF and JJA), cpc.ncep.noaa.gov/products/analysis_monitoring/impacts

items.name: Russia and Central Asia
items.countries: European Russia, Siberia, Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Turkmenistan, Tajikistan, Kyrgyzstan

SON.note: No reliable signal for the autumn sowing of winter wheat.

DJF.note: Winters in European Russia tend to be milder in El Niño years, but the effect is small next to the Atlantic and Arctic drivers and does not repeat reliably.

MAM.note: Central Asia (Kazakhstan to Tajikistan) tends towards a wetter winter and spring, which is favourable for the grain crop; for Russia itself the spring signal is not distinguishable from noise.

vulnerability.note: Russia and Kazakhstan are among the largest wheat exporters: what matters for the world is their harvest, not their imports. A poor Black Sea crop is the single fastest route from weather to global bread prices.

actions: Flood preparedness: drainage, protect stored grain, health measures for water-borne disease, early warning for river basins.
sources: ENSO signal over Russia and Central Asia is weak and season-dependent: Brönnimann 2007; NOAA CPC composite maps; Central Asian winter-spring precipitation response documented in regional studies (Barlow et al.)
NOAA CPC, El Niño and La Niña: typical global impacts (warm-episode maps, DJF and JJA), cpc.ncep.noaa.gov/products/analysis_monitoring/impacts

regions.method: level = round(0.6 × impact + 0.4 × vulnerability + scenario), clipped to 1–5; impact: robust 4, likely 3, weak 1.5, none 0; scenario: base +0 (the event as in the combined forecast), strong +0.5 (top of the model spread), record +1 (reality above every model); one point lower everywhere if the combined peak is below 1.5 °C.

coupling.note: El Niño is a coupling of ocean and air, not a warm patch of water. These three say whether the air is answering: pressure across the Pacific, the cloud tower over the date line, and the trade winds. When they stop answering, the teleconnections that carry the event to harvests stop with them.

fuel.note: Warm water volume is the fuel gauge: the heat piled up in the upper 300 m of the equatorial Pacific before it reaches the surface. It leads the surface index, so it answers the one question the models only guess at — whether the event still has something to grow on. The lead is measured on our own data, not assumed.

layers.after_note: The dashed levels are what each floor reached in the year AFTER the peak of a past strong El Nino - that is when the atmosphere answers. Being below them today is normal: this event has not peaked yet.
layers.note: Four floors of the atmosphere, from satellites. The ocean heats the troposphere with a delay of several months — the delay here is measured against our own Niño 3.4 series, not taken from a textbook. The stratosphere does the opposite: during a strong El Niño it cools, which is why its correlation is weak or negative.

onset_paths.note: Each commodity as a percentage of its price in the onset month, this event against the same months after the onset of the strongest past events. The aggregate FAO index fell after the past onsets for reasons outside the weather; the commodities El Niño touches by name did not necessarily follow it.

risk_core.note: The comparable core of the risk index: only the rules that can be evaluated for past events too - strength of the weekly Nino 3.4, the east-minus-west contrast, the rank of the 30-day mean among all years, and the rise over eight weeks. The full index on this page also counts the model plume, food prices, the atmosphere and the subsurface, none of which exist for 1982 in our form, so the core is always the smaller number. Core against core is a fair comparison; core against the full index is not.

roni_scale.note: RONI at the same season of each event: the tropical mean anomaly is subtracted, so the warm background of the 2020s no longer inflates today's number. The event peaks are the maximum RONI from JAS of the onset year to FMA of the next; ONI peaks alongside for reference.

oisst.source: NOAA OISST v2.1 NRT (ncdcOisst21NrtAgg_LonPM180) via CoastWatch ERDDAP, box means computed by us
oisst.clim: own 1991–2020 daily climatology from the final OISST grid, 15-day smoothing
oisst.note: Direct from the NOAA grid, one day behind. The preliminary (NRT) values of the last two weeks are revised by NOAA later, so the last days can move by a few hundredths. The Niño 3.4 box is checked every day against climatereanalyzer on the days both have.

tao.source: TAO/TRITON moorings (NOAA PMEL) via CoastWatch ERDDAP, daily temperature by depth
tao.clim: own 1991–2020 climatology per mooring, by day of year and depth, 31-day smoothing
tao.note: Each mooring reports temperature at a dozen depths every day. The anomaly is against that mooring's own thirty-year record for the same days of the year, so gaps in the record widen the uncertainty but do not bias it. The 20 °C isotherm marks the thermocline: deeper in the east means the warm layer has arrived there.

godas.source: GODAS ocean reanalysis (NCEP) via NOAA PSL OPeNDAP, monthly, potential temperature
godas.clim: own 1991–2020 monthly climatology on the same grid
godas.note: A reanalysis is a model that assimilates the moorings, Argo floats and satellites into one continuous field. It lags about six weeks and smooths the extremes; the moorings above are the raw measurement, this is the filled-in picture between them.

heat_content.note: mean temperature anomaly of the upper 300 m across the central and eastern equatorial Pacific — the CPC upper-ocean heat content index, recomputed on our climatology

era5.source: ERA5 10 m wind via Open-Meteo archive (hourly → daily zonal mean), six equatorial points 130°E–180°
era5.clim: own 1991–2020 climatology by day of year, 31-day smoothing; σ of the daily anomaly 2.057
era5.note: Westerly is positive. A burst is a westerly anomaly of two sigma or more for five days or longer, averaged over the six points: that is what launches a Kelvin wave, and its warm water reaches the American coast two to three months later. Reanalysis winds at 850 hPa would be the textbook choice, but NCEP's daily files are frozen at March 2026; the 10 m ERA5 wind carries the same bursts at about half the amplitude.

wind.note: ERA5 is the field, the moorings are the check: two independent measures of the same wind.

sea.title: Persian Gulf
sea.note: The box 24–30°N, 48–56°E of the same NOAA grid; the anomaly is against the box's own 1991–2020 climatology. Above 35 °C desalination intakes and fisheries are under stress; the count is of days in the last 120.

kuwait.source: ERA5 via Open-Meteo archive (free, no key), daily, one to three days behind
kuwait.clim: own 1991–2020 climatology for the same point

winter.claim: In an El Niño winter the storm track over the Gulf and Iran is stronger and the storms are wetter; the risk is a wet winter with flash floods, not a forecast of one.

ohc_700.src: NOAA NCEI, 3-month means, anomaly from the 1955–2006 mean

ohc_2000.title: Ocean heat content, 0–2000 m
ohc_2000.src: NOAA NCEI, 3-month means, anomaly from the 1955–2006 mean

mei.title: Multivariate ENSO Index v2
mei.note: Five fields in one index: pressure, wind, temperature of sea and air, cloudiness. Bimonthly, so its last value is a two-month mean. Independent of our three-sign coupling score.

dmi.title: Indian Ocean Dipole (DMI)
dmi.note: West minus east of the tropical Indian Ocean. A positive dipole with an El Niño usually means a drier Indian monsoon and a dry southern Australian autumn — rice and wheat, the two grains Kuwait imports — and a wetter East Africa.

roni.note: RONI is the Niño 3.4 anomaly minus the mean anomaly of the whole tropics (20°S–20°N). NOAA switched its classification to it in February 2026 because a warm tropical ocean makes the plain ONI overstate how strongly the atmosphere is being pushed. The gap between the two is the warm background this event runs on.

background.note: Background means the state the whole system is in while this event runs: how much heat the ocean holds below the surface and how far the planet is out of energy balance. Neither is an El Niño measure, and both are why the statistical models trained on the past keep running low.

mjo.src: NOAA PSL ROMI (real-time OMI from CPC OLR), daily
mjo.note: The Madden–Julian Oscillation is a pulse of cloud and wind that circles the tropics every 30–60 days. Phases 6–8 put its westerly winds over the western Pacific, and that is where the wind bursts that feed an El Niño cluster. Amplitude below 1 means no organised pulse.

summary.verdict: ALERT: Niño 3 is above anything measured at +3.4 °C against the previous maximum +3.3, and water +11.3 °C above normal is sitting at 100 m depth at 125°W. World food prices are the highest in five years, with the FAO index at 133.3.

turning_point.why: The key patch of the Pacific is still warming: the fourteen-day slope is positive 0.024 and acceleration is positive 0.008, with all of the last 30 days setting records.

summary.changed: No new daily observations arrived: Niño 3.4 and world ocean still end on 2026-09-03, and land+ocean still ends on 2026-08-28. The series did not move since the last update.
summary.outlook_2_3w: Over the next two to three weeks the key patch is forecast to stay near 2.705 °C as the median, with a 10% chance of 2.286 °C or lower and a 10% chance of 3.102 °C or higher; the analogue median is 2.881 °C. The world ocean is forecast at a median 0.785 °C, with a 10% edge of 0.694 and a 90% edge of 0.848. Land plus ocean is forecast at a median 0.883 °C, with a 10% edge of 0.682 and a 90% edge of 1.059.
watch: The key patch of the Pacific crossing the analogue median 2.881 or the 90th forecast edge 3.102, because that would mean it is outpacing the analogue path.
The water at 125°W, 100 m depth moving above 11.27 °C, or the warm water volume dropping from its record share without discharging, which would signal how much fuel remains.
A new westerly wind burst in the next two weeks: the last burst ended 2026-08-21 and active_now is false, with the MJO in phase 3 at amplitude 1.19 and not in the burst window.
The next IRI issue raising the combined peak above 3.25 or increasing the 10 of 26 models that are already below reality.
The easternmost Pacific index Niño 1+2 staying near 4.2 °C and crossing its historical maximum 4.5, which would mean the eastern warming continues.
summary.confidence_why: The forecast median for the key patch is 2.705 °C and even the low 10th forecast edge is 2.286 °C, above the 2 °C very strong threshold, so the event is not forecast to weaken below very strong in the next two to three weeks.
caveats: The land+ocean series lags by 7 days, ending 2026-08-28, while Niño 3.4 and world ocean are 1 day old.

The current Niño 3.4 level is already above every analogue on the same days, and the additive peak estimate is 3.24 to 4.51, beyond the record 3.02, so no exact peak can be put on the event; only when the growth stops can be discussed.
The 14-day forecast uses only 44 analogues for Niño 3.4 and 86 for land+ocean, so the p10 to p90 range is wide.

blocks.C: Niño 3.4, the patch of ocean by which El Niño is judged, sits at a 30-day average of 2.59 °C; that is above the same 30 days of all analogues (1982: 0.86, 1997: 1.84, 2015: 1.74, 2023: 1.41) and ranks first among all 45 years since 1982. NOAA's official three-month measure ONI is 1.8 for June–August 2026, above the same season of all analogues (1982: 0.78, 1997: 1.48, 2015: 1.44, 2023: 1.0). The type is eastern Pacific, canonical, with Niño 3 at 3.4 °C and the easternmost index Niño 1+2 at 4.2 °C.
blocks.D: The risk index is 100 of 100. Level 5 risks: a very strong El Niño is already measured, with water in the key patch 2.6 °C warmer than normal versus a very strong threshold of 2 °C; the subsurface fuel is at a record and has not started to burn; water +11.3 °C above normal is sitting at 100 m under 125°W. Level 4 risks say the event has room to grow for 8–16 weeks because the analogues peaked in winter, and the world ocean has set 30 consecutive daily records.
blocks.E: The IRI, a digest of 26 forecast models from the August 2026 issue, has a combined peak 3.25 °C. Against the current weekly reality 2.6 °C for August–October, 10 of 26 models are already below reality. The revision from July 2026 raised the peak from 2.95 to 3.25, with 25 models raised and 0 lowered; the combined peak history has risen from 0.07 in August 2025 to 3.25 in August 2026, so the winter numbers should be read as a lower bound.
blocks.G: The key patch ended the last day at 2.654 °C, with a 7-day mean of 2.613 and a 30-day mean of 2.586; all of the last 30 days set records, and the 14-day slope is a positive 0.024. The 14-day forecast from 2.654 gives a median 2.705, a 10th edge 2.286, and a 90th edge 3.102, with an analogue median 2.881. The world ocean 30-day mean is 0.739 with 30 record days, and land+ocean is 0.832 with 22 records in the last 30 days.
